{% raw %}
`rsh`: run a command or a shell on another computer.

## Synopsis

<strong>rsh</strong> \[<strong>-n</strong>\] <em>host</em> \[<em>command</em>...\]

## Description

<strong>rsh</strong> connects to <strong>rshd</strong>(1) on another computer, over its network cards (TCP, port 514). <em>host</em> is the other computer's name (its <strong>hostname</strong>(1)), or its network card id (<strong>lsdev -i</strong> shows it), whole, or as much of its start as names one computer that answers (rsh asks every rshd in reach, and each answers with its name); a <strong>\*</strong> at its end is allowed. A name said in full wins over an id's start.

With a <em>command</em> (its words joined by spaces), the other computer's <strong>sh -c</strong> runs it. Its input is rsh's (none with <strong>-n</strong>), its output and errors are rsh's, apart, and <strong>rsh</strong> ends as it did: its exit status, or 128 and the signal's number if a signal ended it.

With no command, a login: a shell on a pty on the other computer, as big as this terminal. This terminal goes raw, so every key goes there as it's typed, ^C and the arrows included; a change of this terminal's size (SIGWINCH) goes there too. <strong>~.</strong> at the start of a line disconnects, and <strong>~~</strong> sends one <strong>~</strong>.

## Options

<strong>-n</strong>
: No input for the command (as from <strong>/dev/null</strong>).

## Exit status

The command's, or the shell's; 1 when the host isn't found, the connection fails, or it's lost.

## Examples

```text
rsh 1b9c0e uptime
rsh 1b9c0e
cat notes | rsh 1b9c0e 'cat > /notes'
```

## Notes

Berkeley's r-commands are its model: no passwords and no encryption (anyone whose card reaches the other computer's can do this), which is why their names were kept, and not ssh's. BSD's rsh sent errors on a second connection, never told how the command ended, and ran rlogin when given no command; this one sends everything on one connection, framed, ends as the command did, and logs in itself. It speaks only to mcos's rshd.

## See also

<strong>rshd</strong>(1), <strong>rcp</strong>(1), <strong>rc</strong>(1)
